title: A Problem from Hell: America and the Age of Genocide
author: Samantha Power
target_audience: Students and scholars of history, political science, and international relations
General public interested in American foreign policy and genocide
core_themes: American foreign policy response (or lack thereof) to genocides
Moral responsibility of the US and international community
Role of politicians, diplomats, journalists, and activists
primary_purpose: To examine and critique the United States' response to major genocides of the 20th century, exploring why American leaders and institutions repeatedly failed to intervene to stop genocide despite awareness and moral imperatives.

structure_format.narrative_style: Investigative, analytical, and narrative-driven with journalistic rigor
structure_format.organization: Chronological examination of specific genocides (Armenia, Holocaust, Cambodia, Iraq, Bosnia, Rwanda, Kosovo), analysis of US actions or inaction, and profiles of advocates and decision-makers
features: Analysis of policy documents and official communications
Critical reflection on lessons and missed opportunities

key_concepts_lessons: Genocide is often clearly recognized by governments, but political and bureaucratic obstacles hinder intervention.
Moral outrage does not automatically translate into political will to act.
Activists, journalists, and diplomats can drive attention and advocacy, but lack of institutional support often limits impact.
There are recurring patterns in the US reluctance to engage, including fear of military entanglements, political costs, and prioritization of national interests.
Definitions and denial of genocide are used to evade action.
Prevention and response require both public pressure and institutional readiness.
notable_features: Extensive use of archival research and interviews
Profiles lesser-known advocates and bureaucrats as well as famous politicians
Illuminates moral and political complexities surrounding US intervention
Highlights policy inertia and the consequences of inaction
cultural_historical_context: Written in the immediate aftermath of the 1990s genocides in Bosnia and Rwanda and before the War on Terror, the book interrogates America's track record in confronting mass atrocities since the Armenian Genocide. It reflects broader late-20th and early-21st century debates about human rights, US leadership, and the responsibilities of powerful nations.
reception_impact: Widely acclaimed and influential in policy and academic circles
Won the 2003 Pulitzer Prize for General Non-Fiction
Cited as a foundational text in genocide studies and international relations
Credited with shaping discussions on humanitarian intervention and US foreign policy
Some critics argue it struggles with the balance between idealism and practical politics
